issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s non-bona-fide claim of permanent tenancy is an independent ground for eviction, even without denial of the landlord’s title.
material_facts: The tenant claimed permanent tenancy rights in a reply notice.
The Rent Controller and the Appellate Authority concurrently found that the claim was not bona fide.
issues.conclusion: The non-bona-fide claim of permanent tenancy independently supported eviction; the tenant did not also have to deny the landlord’s title.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10(2)(vi) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent & Eviction) Control Act, 1960 sets out denial of the landlord’s title and a claim of permanent tenancy disjunctively. Either ground, if made without bona fides, is sufficient for eviction.

predicates.tenant_eviction_appeal: A tenant appealed an order directing the tenant’s eviction.
predicates.tenant_claimed_permanent_tenancy: The tenant asserted a right to remain in the premises permanently.
predicates.permanent_tenancy_claim_not_bona_fide: The claim to permanent tenancy was found not to be bona fide.

issues.definition: When a tenant appeals an eviction order after making a non-bona-fide claim to permanent tenancy, that claim independently supports eviction.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s need for non-residential premises for a family business can satisfy the requirement that the premises be needed for the landlord’s business when the business is also the landlord’s business.
material_facts: The premises were sought for a photographic studio operated by the landlord’s son as a family business.
The landlord’s son and the tenant both operated photographic studios.
The Court treated the family business as the landlord’s business as well as the son’s.
issues.conclusion: The landlord’s requirement for the family business satisfied the business-purpose requirement, even assuming the provision was to be construed restrictively.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10(3)(a)(iii) permits recovery of a non-residential building for a business the landlord carries on, or for a business the landlord bona fide proposes to commence. The Court distinguished D.N. Sanghavi & Sons v. Ambalal, which concerned a different statute, and relied on Ballaiah v. Lachaiah in considering the relevance of a family business. It did not need to decide the broader question whether a landlord may recover premises for a family member’s separate business, because the business here was the landlord’s family business as well.

predicates.nonresidential_business_eviction: The proceeding sought eviction from non-residential premises for a business purpose.
predicates.premises_required_for_family_business: The landlord sought the premises for a business operated as a family business.
predicates.family_business_is_also_landlords_busine: The landlord’s business interests included the family business for which the premises were sought.

issues.definition: In an eviction proceeding concerning non-residential premises, a need for a family business that is also the landlord’s business satisfies the landlord-business requirement.

issues.legal_issue: Ownership of other premises does not bar recovery of non-residential premises when those other premises are used for residence and are not suitable for the business for which recovery is sought.
material_facts: The landlord owned a house containing four shop portions.
The fact-finders found that the portions had not been used as shops and had been used for residential purposes.
The portions were in a non-commercial area and were found not to be suitable for the business at issue.
The landlord’s family business was being conducted in rented premises in the same locality as the premises sought.
issues.conclusion: The landlord’s ownership of the other premises did not bar recovery because those portions were used for residence rather than as non-residential business premises and were unsuitable for the business.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10(3)(a)(iii) requires that, for the relevant business purpose, the landlord not be occupying another non-residential building that is the landlord’s own or one to whose possession the landlord is entitled. The Court treated the actual use and suitability of the other premises as relevant to whether they were non-residential premises for the business. It considered Ballaiah v. Lachaiah and rejected the contention, based on L. Chettiar v. K. Subbarayan, that ownership of other business premises invariably precludes recovery; the factual findings supported the conclusion that the other portions did not bar recovery.

rule.if: nonresidential_business_eviction and landlord_owns_other_premises and other_premises_used_for_residence and other_premises_not_suitable_for_business

predicates.nonresidential_business_eviction: The proceeding sought eviction from non-residential premises for a business purpose.
predicates.landlord_owns_other_premises: The landlord owned other premises in the relevant locality.
predicates.other_premises_used_for_residence: The other premises were being used for residential purposes rather than as shops.
predicates.other_premises_not_suitable_for_business: The other premises were found unsuitable for the business for which the landlord sought the premises.

issues.definition: In a business-purpose eviction proceeding, ownership of other premises used for residence and unsuitable for the business does not bar recovery.
